<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

steps.message: The evidence supports a clear distinction: the run completed without numerical failure, but the fused training path used incorrect token targets. I’m writing the diagnosis with source references, the CPU probe result, and the validation trends. I’ll also note what this recording cannot establish without a corrected comparison.

arguments.input:
text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /logs/artifacts/agent_answer.md
+**The training computation is incorrect, despite a numerically stable, completed run.** The principal implementation issue is a token-target alignment bug in the **Qwen3-VL fused Torch log-probability path under Ulysses sequence parallelism**: hidden states are sliced by SP rank, but the fused head receives the full sequence of target IDs. Both SP ranks consume the first shard's targets. Consequently, much of the second shard's policy loss and gradient concerns the wrong tokens. High rewards and an initial validation improvement do not establish computation correctness.
+
+The recorded configuration activates precisely this path: four GPUs, FSDP size four, SP size two, padding removal, fused kernels with the Torch backend, and `trainer.use_legacy_worker_impl=disable` ([configuration](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:16), [model options](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:384), [worker selection](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:831)). The separate sequence-parallel mesh is DP2×SP2; the FSDP mesh is four-way FULL_SHARD ([mesh construction](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:196), [sharding selection](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/utils.py:38)). The console confirms both the Qwen3-VL input-slicing patch and the Torch fused backend on all four workers, for example [lines 862 onward](/workspace/logs/console.log:862). This is an exercised implementation defect, not merely an unused branch.
+
+The source establishes the failure as follows:
+
+1. [FSDPEngineWithLMHead.prepare_model_inputs](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:914) packs the tokens and computes the correct next-token targets with `torch.roll(..., shifts=-1)` at line 924. For a vision-language model, it **pads but does not slice the input IDs**, because image embedding insertion needs the full input. It separately pads and slices the shifted targets at lines 943–947.
+2. Those correct local targets are stored in `output_args["input_ids_rmpad_rolled"]`. However, [the model-input construction](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:955) never passes them as `labels`; the fused extra arguments at lines 1012–1018 contain only temperature and `return_dict`. Thus computing the right targets here does not make the fused computation correct.
+3. [The VLM Ulysses wrapper](/workspace/framework/verl/models/transformers/monkey_patch.py:164) slices `inputs_embeds`, position IDs, visual masks and visual features before the text model. Its output hidden states therefore have local sequence length, while the outer Qwen3-VL forward still has the full padded `input_ids`.
+4. [Qwen3-VL's fused Torch forward](/workspace/framework/verl/models/transformers/qwen3_vl.py:278) receives no `labels`, so it rolls the **full** input IDs at line 294 and passes them with the **local** hidden states to `FusedLinearForPPO` at lines 298–304.
+5. [FusedLinearForPPOFunction.forward](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:99) checks dimensionality but not equal token counts. It sets `T = hidden_states.shape[0]` after flattening and loops only over that local `T`, indexing `input_ids[chunk_start:chunk_end]` from zero on every rank. It silently consumes the first `T` targets on both ranks. [The output path](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:1033) trusts these fused log-probabilities and gathers them; only the unfused branch uses the correct local targets. Gathering and response masking restore the expected shape, not the missing target alignment.
+
+For a packed sequence of length `2T`, let hidden state `h_i` predict token `x_(i+1)`. Ignoring terminal/padding positions:
+
+| SP rank | Hidden states | Required targets | Targets actually consumed |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| 0 | `h_0 … h_(T-1)` | `x_1 … x_T` | `x_1 … x_T` |
+| 1 | `h_T … h_(2T-1)` | `x_(T+1) …` | `x_1 … x_T` |
+
+The second shard therefore computes, for local position `j`, `log p(x_(j+1) | h_(T+j))` instead of the sampled next token's log-probability. This affects interior response positions, not just padding or a single shard boundary. Packed batches can even supply a target from a different example. It does not imply exactly half of *unmasked response* tokens are wrong: that depends on packing, prompt masks and coincidentally equal token IDs.
+
+I verified the indexing with a small CPU probe executing the supplied Qwen3-VL fused-forward function and fused-head implementation, using synthetic hidden states and the PyTorch cross-entropy fallback. No model training or optimizer step was performed. For input IDs `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]`, two four-position shards, and logits that favor each true next token by 10:
+
+- Rank 0 consumes `[1,2,3,4]` and agrees with the correctly aligned computation: approximately `-0.000318` per token.
+- Rank 1 should consume `[5,6,7,0]` but consumes `[1,2,3,4]`: approximately `-10.000318` per token instead of `-0.000318`.
+- All outputs remain finite and gather to the expected eight-position shape. At rank 1's first position, the gradient of the returned log-probability increases token 1 and decreases the correct token 5. The source's backward pass uses these same erroneous target IDs ([gradient construction](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:68), [chunk indexing](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:171)). This demonstrates an objective/gradient error, not merely incorrect logging.
+
+Both old-policy recomputation and actor training use this engine ([worker methods](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine_workers.py:635)). PPO then exponentiates `log_prob - old_log_prob` and applies the response's GRPO advantage to it ([loss](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:1329)). Even if the same erroneous target appears in both evaluations and the ratio initially equals one, its gradient remains a gradient for the wrong action. Moreover, old log-probabilities are computed over the rollout batch, whereas actor updates split it into minibatches and dynamically repack each one ([old/update paths](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py:1185), [packing](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/utils.py:74)); the wrong target can change with packing. This can create apparent policy differences unrelated to a change in the probability of the sampled action.
+
+The scalar evidence is consistent with an unhealthy objective but does not independently prove its cause. At step 1, `actor/ppo_kl=0.420173`, `pg_clipfrac=0.145752`, and `pg_clipfrac_lower=0.033331`; across the run, PPO KL ranges from 0.117654 to 0.593388 ([step 1](/workspace/logs/scalars.jsonl:2), [complete history](/workspace/logs/scalars.jsonl:1)). Here `ppo_kl` is the masked old/current log-probability difference, not divergence from a reference model. Reference KL loss and KL reward shaping are disabled. Also, a logged step aggregates four PPO minibatch updates (`128×8` responses divided by `32×8`), so step 1 is not a pristine, no-update equality test. These diagnostics are themselves contaminated by the target bug.
+
+Numerically and operationally, the session completed as intended. All numeric scalar values in the 41 records are finite.
